questions.q: What does the no-cloning theorem actually forbid?
options: Any unitary operation taking an arbitrary, unknown qubit state and a blank qubit to two independent copies of that state, for every possible input state
Preparing two qubits in the same known state from scratch
Measuring a qubit more than once
Entangling two qubits together
questions.explain: No-cloning specifically forbids a universal cloner that works for every unknown input state. If you already know the state, you can always prepare a second copy from that knowledge -- that's not what's forbidden.

questions.q: In the proof, applying the hypothetical cloning unitary U to |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 produces (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 by linearity. Why does this contradict U being a correct cloning machine?
options: A correct clone of |+⟩ should produce the product state (|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)/2, which has different coefficients (0.5 on all four terms) than the entangled result (1/√2≈0.707 on only two terms) -- they are provably different states
Because (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 is not a normalized state
Because linearity only applies to classical bits, not qubits
There is no actual contradiction; both results are equally valid clones
questions.explain: Direct comparison of coefficients shows the two results are genuinely different states (verified): the entangled result has zero amplitude on |01⟩ and |10⟩, while the correct product-state clone has 0.5 on every term, including those.

questions.q: Why is no-cloning considered a fundamental impossibility rather than a current engineering limitation?
options: The proof relies only on unitarity (linearity) of quantum operations, with no reference to hardware noise or qubit count -- better engineering can never close a gap that is structural, not technological
Because no quantum hardware has ever attempted to clone a qubit
Because the theorem has only been tested on a small number of qubits so far
It is actually an engineering limitation, expected to be solved as hardware improves
questions.explain: The proof is purely about what linear/unitary operators can do mathematically, independent of any physical implementation detail -- the same category of fact as 'you can't divide by zero', not a limitation current technology might eventually overcome.

questions.q: Why can't you work around no-cloning by just measuring an unknown qubit to learn its full state and then recreating it elsewhere?
options: Measuring an unknown qubit collapses it (destroying the original superposition) and only reveals one probabilistic bit of information, not the full complex amplitudes -- it is exactly as impossible as cloning
Measurement always reveals the full amplitudes a and b with certainty
Measurement has no effect on a qubit's state at all
Measuring a qubit always produces a perfect classical copy of it automatically
questions.explain: Measurement is probabilistic and collapses the state (Chapter 3) -- it gives you one bit of outcome information, not the underlying amplitudes, so it cannot be used to sidestep no-cloning by 'reading off' an unknown state.

questions.q: What is the deeper pattern the no-cloning proof reveals about attempting to copy a superposition?
options: The attempted 'clone' operation, applied via a linear unitary, doesn't fail silently -- it produces a real but different outcome: an entangled state instead of a clean duplicate
The cloning attempt always produces exactly the correct clone, contradicting the theorem
The cloning attempt destroys both qubits entirely, leaving nothing
The cloning attempt only fails for the |0⟩ and |1⟩ basis states, never for superpositions
questions.explain: Linearity forces the result to be (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 -- a real, well-defined entangled state, just not a clone. This is a recurring theme: operations that can't duplicate a superposition often entangle the systems instead.
